entries.lesson_core_move: Formulate the continuous-time convolution integral y(t)=(x*h)(t)=int_{-infty}^{infty} x(tau)h(t-tau) d tau as the LTI system output obtained by integrating weighted, shifted impulse responses.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Definition of Continuous-Time Convolution

image_slots.image_description: A clean LTI-system block diagram showing an input signal x(t) decomposed into infinitesimal weighted impulse contributions x(tau) d tau. Each weighted impulse passes through an LTI system block labeled impulse response h(t), producing a shifted impulse response h(t-tau). Arrows from several shifted responses accumulate into the output y(t). Use simple labels, sparse annotations, and no numerical signal plots.

blocks.text: Continuous-time convolution describes the output of an LTI system from its input and impulse response. The key idea is to view the input $x(t)$ as an accumulation of tiny weighted impulse contributions, one contribution near each input time $\tau$.

The contribution near time $\tau$ has weight $x(\tau)$ d $\tau$. Since the system is LTI, an impulse located at $\tau$ produces a shifted impulse response $h(t-\tau)$, so the weighted contribution to the output at time t is $x(\tau)$$h(t-\tau)$ d $\tau$.
To form the total output at time t, add the contributions from all input times $\tau$. This accumulated output is called the convolution of x and h.

Read this formula as an accumulation of weighted, shifted impulse responses: $x(\tau)$ gives the input weight at time $\tau$, $h(t-\tau)$ gives the corresponding shifted impulse response observed at time t, and d $\tau$ tells us to integrate over all input times. For now, the goal is to formulate and interpret the definition, not to compute overlap intervals or evaluate the integral.

sections.section_title: Reading the Signals in the Convolution Definition

example_content.example_prompt: In $y(t)$=$\int$_{-$\infty$}^{$\infty$} $x(\tau)$$h(t-\tau)$\,d$\tau$, identify the input term, the shifted impulse-response term, the integration variable, and the output.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the convolution definition itself. We are not evaluating the integral yet; we are reading the parts of the formula and naming what each part represents.
The output is $y(t)$. It names the value produced by the LTI system at the fixed observation time t.
The integration variable is $\tau$. The differential d $\tau$ tells us that $\tau$ is the variable being swept through all input times inside the integral.
The input term is $x(\tau)$. For each input time $\tau$, this factor gives the input weight attached to the contribution from that time.
The shifted impulse-response term is $h(t-\tau)$. It is the response observed at time t from an impulse placed at the input time $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.latex: y(t):\text{ output},\quad \tau:\text{ integration variable},\quad x(\tau):\text{ input term},\quad h(t-\tau):\text{ shifted impulse-response term}

explanation_blocks.text: So the formula says to accumulate input-weighted shifted impulse responses. This example only labels the roles of the symbols; it does not choose limits from signal support or compute the integral.

sections.section_title: Writing the Continuous-Time Convolution Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Given an LTI system with input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$, write the convolution integral for the output $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the system is LTI and the input and impulse response are named. For an LTI system, the output is the convolution of the input with the impulse response.
To write the integral form, use $\tau$ as the integration variable. The input term becomes $x(\tau)$, because $\tau$ scans the input time.
The impulse-response term becomes $h(t-\tau)$, because an impulse located at time $\tau$ contributes a shifted response observed at the output time t.
Finally, include the full accumulation over all input times. That means the limits run from negative infinity to infinity and the differential is d $\tau$.
This is the complete convolution setup for the named input and impulse response. The result writes the output formula; it does not yet evaluate the integral.

sections.section_title: Connecting the Integral to an LTI System Output

example_content.example_prompt: An LTI system has input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$. Express its output $y(t)$ using the continuous-time convolution definition.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the system is LTI and its impulse response is $h(t)$. For an LTI system, the impulse response tells how the system responds to each shifted impulse in the input.
Use the input $x(t)$ as the source of weights. A contribution from input time $\tau$ has weight $x(\tau)$, and the corresponding shifted impulse response is $h(t-\tau)$.
So the output is the convolution of the input with the impulse response.
Writing out the convolution definition gives the accumulated contribution from all input times $\tau$.
This expression is the LTI system output. It is an accumulation of weighted, shifted impulse responses, not pointwise multiplication of $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ and not the impulse response alone.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Convolution as Accumulated Shifted Responses

example_content.example_prompt: Explain what $x(\tau)$$h(t-\tau)$\,d$\tau$ contributes to $y(t)$ in the convolution integral.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the differential contribution inside the convolution integral. The expression $x(\tau)$$h(t-\tau)$ d $\tau$ is not the entire output; it describes one small contribution to the output from input times near $\tau$.

First read $x(\tau)$ d $\tau$ as the small weighted input contribution near the input time $\tau$. The value $x(\tau)$ gives the weight, and d $\tau$ represents the tiny interval of input time being included.
Because the system is LTI, an impulse located at time $\tau$ produces the shifted impulse response $h(t-\tau)$. At the output time t, the value of that shifted response is $h(t-\tau)$.
Multiplying these pieces gives the contribution to $y(t)$ from that one small slice of input time: the input weight times the shifted response value.
The full convolution integral accumulates all of these small shifted-response contributions over every input time $\tau$.
So $x(\tau)$$h(t-\tau)$ d $\tau$ is one infinitesimal shifted-response contribution, and the integral is the accumulated output $y(t)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Distinguish tau as the integration variable that scans input and impulse-response overlap from t as the output time in the continuous-time convolution integral.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Meaning of the Dummy Variable $\tau$

blocks.text: In the continuous-time convolution integral, the two time symbols have different jobs. The symbol $t$ names the output time, while the integral scans through input-time locations using $\tau$.
The differential $d\tau$ tells you that $\tau$ is the variable of integration. As the integral runs, $\tau$ sweeps through the possible input-time values.
For a chosen output time $t$, the factor $x(\tau)$ reads the input value at the scanning time $\tau$. The factor $h(t-\tau)$ reads the shifted impulse-response value paired with that same $\tau$.

blocks.latex: \text{integrate with respect to }\tau,\quad \text{leave a function of }t

blocks.text: After the integration is complete, $\tau$ has been summed out, so it should not remain as a free variable. The result is an output value or output formula indexed by $t$.

sections.section_title: Identifying $\tau$ as the Variable of Integration

example_content.example_prompt: In $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, identify the variable of integration and the notation that tells you.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the integral notation. To find the variable of integration, look at the differential at the end of the integrand.
The differential is $d\tau$, so the integral is taken with respect to $\tau$. That means $\tau$ is the symbol being swept through the integral.
The symbol $t$ is not being integrated here. It labels the output time in $y(t)$ and stays fixed while $\tau$ scans through the integral.
Therefore, $\tau$ is the dummy variable of integration, and $d\tau$ is the notation that tells you.

sections.section_title: Reading $x(\tau)$ Along the Scanning Time Axis

image_slots.image_description: Clean schematic continuous-time signal plot labeled $x(\tau)$. The horizontal axis is labeled $\tau$ with tick marks at $-1$, $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, and $5$. The vertical amplitude axis has a tick at $2$. Plot a rectangular input signal with $x(\tau)=2$ for $0\le \tau\le 4$ and $x(\tau)=0$ outside that interval, using vertical edges at $\tau=0$ and $\tau=4$. Mark the tick at $\tau=2$ clearly. Do not include extra signals, overlap shading, or decorative styling.

example_content.example_prompt: Use the plotted signal $x(\tau)$ to read $x(2)$ and identify the interval of $\tau$ values where $x(\tau)$ is nonzero.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the axis label. Because the horizontal axis is labeled $\tau$, each horizontal location is a scanning-time value for the input signal $x(\tau)$.
To read $x(2)$, locate $\tau=2$ on the horizontal axis and read the height of the plotted signal at that location. The graph has height $2$ there, so $x(2)=2$.

To identify where $x(\tau)$ is nonzero, scan along the $\tau$ axis and look for where the plotted signal is not on the zero line. The signal is above zero from $\tau=0$ through $\tau=4$ and is zero outside that interval.
So reading $x(\tau)$ means reading the input signal along the scanning $\tau$ axis: at $\tau=2$ the input value is $2$, and the visible nonzero interval is $0\le \tau\le 4$.

sections.section_title: Reading $h(t-\tau)$ Along the Same $\tau$ Axis

image_slots.image_description: Clean schematic impulse-response plot labeled $h(u)$. The horizontal axis is labeled $u$ with tick marks at $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$, and $4$. The vertical amplitude axis has ticks at $1$ and $3$. Plot a piecewise-constant impulse response with $h(u)=1$ for $0\le u<2$, $h(u)=3$ for $2\le u\le 4$, and $h(u)=0$ outside that interval. Add a small note above the plot: fixed $t=4$. Add two unobtrusive mapping annotations: $\tau=1\Rightarrow u=4-1=3$ pointing to $u=3$, and $\tau=3\Rightarrow u=4-3=1$ pointing to $u=1$. Do not include $x(\tau)$, overlap shading, a flipped graph, or decorative styling.

example_content.example_prompt: For fixed $t=4$, use the plotted impulse response $h(u)$ to read $h(t-\tau)$ at $\tau=1$ and $\tau=3$.

explanation_blocks.text: The new cue is the argument of $h$. Since the plotted impulse response is $h(u)$, first convert each scanning value $\tau$ into the input argument $u=t-\tau$, then read the height of $h(u)$ at that $u$ value.
For $\tau=1$, the argument of $h$ is $u=4-1=3$. On the plotted $h(u)$ signal, the height at $u=3$ is $3$, so $h(t-\tau)$ has value $3$ at $\tau=1$.
For $\tau=3$, the argument of $h$ is $u=4-3=1$. On the same plotted $h(u)$ signal, the height at $u=1$ is $1$, so $h(t-\tau)$ has value $1$ at $\tau=3$.
Thus the same scanning values of $\tau$ are used, but $h$ is read at the transformed argument $t-\tau$. For fixed $t=4$, the requested values are $3$ at $\tau=1$ and $1$ at $\tau=3$.

sections.section_title: Distinguishing the Scanning Variable $\tau$ from the Output Time $t$

example_content.example_prompt: In $y(3)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(3-\tau)\,d\tau$, identify what scans during integration and what output time is being computed.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue for what scans is the differential at the end of the integral. Since the differential is $d\tau$, the integration is with respect to $\tau$.
The expression $y(3)$ asks for the output at one specific time. That means the output-time value is fixed at $3$ while the integral runs.
The factor $h(3-\tau)$ changes as the integral scans because $\tau$ changes. The number $3$ does not scan; it stays fixed as the output time being computed.
So during this integration, $\tau$ scans through the input-time axis, and the output time being computed is $t=3$, which is the value named by $y(3)$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing That Integration Over $\tau$ Leaves a Function of $t$

example_content.example_prompt: Explain why $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ can still be a function of $t$ after the integration over $\tau$ is complete.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the differential $d\tau$. It tells you that the integral is taken with respect to $\tau$, so $\tau$ is the dummy variable being summed out.
A dummy variable does not remain as a free variable after integration. Once the integration over $\tau$ is complete, the result should not still depend on $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.latex: \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau \quad \text{integrates out }\tau\text{ and leaves an output indexed by }t

explanation_blocks.text: The symbol $t$ is different: it is a parameter in the integrand, not the variable named by the differential. While $\tau$ is scanned and summed out, $t$ remains as the output-time label.
Therefore, integrating over $\tau$ removes the dummy variable $\tau$ but can leave a result that depends on $t$. That is why the output is written as $y(t)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Treat t as a fixed output-time parameter while letting tau vary to set up the convolution integrand x(tau)h(t-tau) for a continuous-time LTI system.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Holding $t$ Fixed During Convolution

blocks.text: In the convolution integral, $t$ and $\tau$ do different jobs. The symbol $t$ names the output time, and $\tau$ is the integration variable that scans through input time.

To find one output value, choose one value of $t$ and hold it fixed. Then let $\tau$ run through the integral. During that one integral, $t$ is not another variable of integration; it is the chosen output time.
After fixing $t=t_0$, the input factor stays $x(\tau)$, and the impulse-response factor becomes $h(t_0-\tau)$. Both factors are now read as functions of $\tau$ for that chosen output time.

The result is one $\tau$-dependent integrand. Integrating it over $\tau$ produces the single output value $y(t_0)$. Choosing another output time means holding a new value of $t$ fixed and forming a new integrand.

sections.section_title: Substituting a Fixed Output Time into $h(t-\tau)$

example_content.example_prompt: For $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, rewrite $h(t-\tau)$ when the output time is fixed at $t=3$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the fixed output time $t=3$. In $h(t-\tau)$, substitute $3$ only for $t$ and leave $\tau$ as the variable.
So the shifted impulse-response factor becomes $h(3-\tau)$. Now use the formula for $h$: whatever argument is inside $h(\cdot)$ replaces the argument in $e^{-(\cdot)}u(\cdot)$.

Thus, for the fixed output time $t=3$, $h(t-\tau)$ is rewritten as $e^{-(3-\tau)}u(3-\tau)$. The expression still depends on $\tau$, so it is ready to be used as a $\tau$-varying factor in the convolution setup.

sections.section_title: Forming $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ with $t$ Fixed

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(\tau)=\tau u(\tau)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, form $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ for fixed output time $t=2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the fixed output time $t=2$. First rewrite the impulse-response factor by substituting $2$ only for $t$ in $h(t-\tau)$.
Now use the formula $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$. The argument of $h$ is $2-\tau$, so replace the argument in the exponential and in the unit step with $2-\tau$.
The input factor is already written as a function of $\tau$, so it stays $x(\tau)=\tau u(\tau)$. Form the integrand by multiplying this factor by the rewritten impulse-response factor.
The final integrand contains $\tau$ but no free $t$. That means $t$ has been fixed at $2$, while $\tau$ remains the variable for the convolution setup.

sections.section_title: Comparing the Integrand for Different Fixed Values of $t$

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(\tau)=u(\tau)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, form and compare $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$ for fixed output times $t=1$ and $t=4$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that two different output times are being checked. Form one $\tau$-dependent integrand for $t=1$, then form a separate $\tau$-dependent integrand for $t=4$.
For $t=1$, substitute $1$ into the impulse-response factor and keep the input factor as $x(\tau)=u(\tau)$.
For $t=4$, repeat the same process with $4$ as the fixed output time. The input factor $u(\tau)$ does not change.

The only change is the fixed output-time value inside the impulse-response factor: $1-\tau$ becomes $4-\tau$. In both integrands, $\tau$ is still the only variable left, and the input factor $u(\tau)$ stays the same.

sections.section_title: Recognizing $\tau$ as the Only Variable Left to Integrate

example_content.example_prompt: Decide whether $x(\tau)h(3-\tau)=\tau e^{-(3-\tau)}u(\tau)u(3-\tau)$ is ready to integrate over $\tau$, and explain what variable remains.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that this is a readiness check, not an evaluation problem. Inspect the expression for any remaining free $t$.
There is no free $t$ left in the expression. The appearance of $3-\tau$ shows that the output time has already been fixed at $t=3$.
Every nonconstant part of the integrand depends on $\tau$: $\tau$, $u(\tau)$, $3-\tau$, and $u(3-\tau)$. So $\tau$ is the only variable left to scan during integration.
Therefore, the expression is ready to integrate over $\tau$ to compute the one output value $y(3)$. The setup stops here; evaluating the integral is a separate step.

entries.lesson_core_move: Rewrite each signal's formula and active time interval using tau as the integration variable so it can be placed correctly in the continuous-time convolution integral.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Rewriting Signals as Functions of $\tau$

blocks.text: In continuous-time convolution, $\tau$ is the variable that scans across the input timeline, while $t$ stays fixed as the output-time parameter. That is why the signals inside the convolution integral are written as functions of $\tau$.

To rewrite a signal in $\tau$, replace the independent variable in both places where the signal uses time: the formula and the active interval. Keep the constants, coefficients, endpoint values, and inequality directions the same.
This rewrite only prepares the signal for the convolution integral. It does not find overlap intervals, choose integration bounds, or evaluate the convolution.

sections.section_title: Replacing $t$ with $\tau$ in Signal Formulas

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite the signal formula $x(t)=3t+1$ as a function of $\tau$ for convolution setup.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the signal is still written with $t$, but convolution setup needs the input signal written on the $\tau$ axis. Here we are only rewriting the formula, so there is no active interval to change yet.
Start with the original formula.
Replace the independent variable $t$ with $\tau$. The coefficient $3$, the constant $1$, and the addition stay unchanged.

So the convolution-ready version of the formula is $x(\tau)=3\tau+1$. This step only changes the independent variable inside the signal formula; it does not introduce $t-\tau$ or choose any integration bounds.

sections.section_title: Rewriting Active Time Intervals with $\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite the formula and active interval for $x(t)=4-t$ active on $1\le t\le 5$ using $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the signal is described in two places using $t$: the formula and the active interval. For convolution setup, both parts need to be written using the integration variable $\tau$.
First replace $t$ with $\tau$ in the formula. Then replace the interval variable $t$ with $\tau$. The endpoint numbers $1$ and $5$ stay the same, and the inequality directions stay the same.
So the prepared signal is $x(\tau)=4-\tau$ active on $1\le \tau\le 5$. This step only rewrites the signal in the integration variable; it does not find overlap intervals or choose convolution bounds.

sections.section_title: Rewriting Shifted Signal Formulas with $\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $x(t)=e^{-2(t-1)}$ active for $t\ge 1$ as a function of $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted group $(t-1)$ inside the formula. Since this is still the original signal $x(t)$, the rewrite changes the signal's independent variable from $t$ to $\tau$ while preserving the shift structure.
Replace $t$ with $\tau$ inside the grouped expression, so $(t-1)$ becomes $(\tau-1)$. Do not change the shift constant or reverse the order inside the parentheses.
Then rewrite the active interval with the same variable change. The condition $t\ge 1$ becomes $\tau\ge 1$.
So the prepared signal is $x(\tau)=e^{-2(\tau-1)}$ active for $\tau\ge 1$. This is a rewrite of the given signal only; it does not introduce the convolution-specific form $t-\tau$.

sections.section_title: Preparing Piecewise Signals in $\tau$ for Convolution Setup

example_content.example_prompt: Prepare the piecewise signal $x(t)=0$ for $t<0$, $x(t)=t$ for $0\le t<2$, $x(t)=2$ for $2\le t\le 4$, and $x(t)=0$ for $t>4$ as a function of $\tau$ for convolution setup.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the signal is piecewise: each row has a formula and a condition. To prepare it for convolution setup, rewrite every row using $\tau$ while keeping the same order, endpoint numbers, endpoint inclusions, and zero pieces.

explanation_blocks.latex: x(t)=\begin{cases}0, & t<0\\ t, & 0\le t<2\\ 2, & 2\le t\le 4\\ 0, & t>4\end{cases}

explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite the formulas first. The constant pieces $0$ and $2$ stay unchanged. The formula $t$ becomes $\tau$ because the independent variable is now $\tau$.
Then rewrite each condition by replacing $t$ with $\tau$. The condition $t<0$ becomes $\tau<0$, $0\le t<2$ becomes $0\le \tau<2$, $2\le t\le 4$ becomes $2\le \tau\le 4$, and $t>4$ becomes $\tau>4$.

So the prepared signal is the complete piecewise definition of $x(\tau)$ above. This step only rewrites the signal description; it does not combine pieces, find overlap, choose integration bounds, or evaluate a convolution.

entries.lesson_core_move: Trace how an input contribution x(tau)d tau at time tau produces the time-invariant system response x(tau)h(t-tau)d tau, justifying h(t-tau) as the impulse response shifted to each impulse location in the convolution integral.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Why $h(t-\tau)$ Appears

blocks.text: Convolution is built by tracking one tiny input contribution at a time. The key question in this lesson is: if an input contribution is located at time $\tau$, what shifted copy of the impulse response does it produce?
Start with the basic impulse-response fact for an LTI system. If the input is the unit impulse at time $0$, the output is the impulse response $h(t)$.
Now move the impulse to a fixed time $\tau_0$. Because the system is time-invariant, shifting the input impulse by $\tau_0$ shifts the output response by the same amount.
In the convolution integral, the impulse location is not one fixed number. The variable $\tau$ scans through all possible input times, so the response to an impulse located at $\tau$ is $h(t-\tau)$.
The input does not contribute a plain unit impulse at time $\tau$. It contributes a small weighted impulse with weight $x(\tau)d\tau$, so the shifted response is scaled by that same weight.

So $h(t-\tau)$ appears because it is the impulse response shifted to match the input contribution located at time $\tau$. The factor $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)d\tau$ is one output contribution, and convolution accumulates all such contributions over every $\tau$.

sections.section_title: Tracing the Response to an Impulse at $\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: For an LTI system with impulse response $h(t)$, identify the output produced by the input $\delta(t-2)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shifted impulse $\delta(t-2)$. This is the unit impulse moved from time $0$ to time $2$.
For this LTI system, the response to the unit impulse at time $0$ is the impulse response $h(t)$.
Because the system is time-invariant, shifting the input impulse by $2$ shifts the output response by the same amount. The shift stays in the same form: $t-2$.
Therefore, the output produced by the input $\delta(t-2)$ is $h(t-2)$.

sections.section_title: Scaling the Shifted Response by $x(\tau)d\tau$

example_content.example_prompt: For an LTI system with impulse response $h(t)$, write the output contribution from the weighted impulse $x(2)\Delta\tau\,\delta(t-2)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is still the shifted impulse $\delta(t-2)$. From the previous section, an unweighted impulse at time $2$ produces the shifted response $h(t-2)$.
Now the impulse is multiplied by the scalar weight $x(2)\Delta\tau$. Because the system is linear, the same scalar multiplies the output response.

Therefore, the output contribution from $x(2)\Delta\tau\,\delta(t-2)$ is $x(2)\Delta\tau\,h(t-2)$. The shift is still determined by the impulse location; the new factor only scales the shifted response.

sections.section_title: Reading $h(t-\tau)$ at a Fixed Output Time

example_content.example_prompt: With the output time fixed at $t=5$, rewrite the shifted impulse-response factor $h(t-\tau)$ as a function of $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the phrase "output time fixed at $t=5$". This means $t$ is held at one output time, while $\tau$ remains the variable input location.
Start with the shifted response factor from the convolution integrand.
Substitute $5$ only for the fixed output time $t$. Do not replace $\tau$, because $\tau$ still scans the possible input locations.
Therefore, with the output time fixed at $t=5$, the response factor becomes $h(5-\tau)$. This is the shifted response value observed at output time $5$ from each input location $\tau$.

sections.section_title: Connecting Weighted Shifted Responses to the Convolution Integrand

example_content.example_prompt: Identify the convolution integrand that comes from accumulating the weighted shifted-response contributions $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)d\tau$ over all input times $\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the word integrand. We are not computing the output yet; we are identifying the expression that will be accumulated over $\tau$.
Start from one output contribution caused by the small input piece at time $\tau$. The input weight is $x(\tau)d\tau$, and the shifted response factor is $h(t-\tau)$.
In this contribution, $d\tau$ is the small accumulation width. The integrand is the factor multiplying that width.
So the convolution integrand is $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)$. It combines the input value at the scanning time with the impulse response shifted to match that same input location.
Accumulating all of these infinitesimal contributions over every $\tau$ gives the LTI output. The integral sign belongs to the full accumulation, not to the integrand by itself.

entries.lesson_core_move: Execute the flip-shift-multiply-integrate procedure by holding t fixed, forming h(t-tau), multiplying it by x(tau), and integrating over tau to set up a continuous-time LTI convolution output.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Flip-Shift-Multiply-Integrate Procedure

image_slots.image_description: A clean four-stage schematic over a horizontal tau-axis using one simple finite-duration input signal x(tau) and one simple finite-duration impulse response h(tau). Show the original input x(tau), the flipped response h(-tau), the shifted flipped response h(t-tau) for one fixed positive value of t marked as fixed, the product signal x(tau)h(t-tau), and an arrow from the shaded product area to y(t). Include an integral arrow labeled int_{-infty}^{infty} dot d tau. The visual should show procedure order only and should not evaluate the integral.

blocks.text: The convolution output at time t is found by building one product on the $\tau$-axis and then integrating that product over $\tau$. In this setup, t is the output time you hold fixed, while $\tau$ is the variable that sweeps across the input timeline.

The flip-shift-multiply-integrate procedure is the concrete way to set up that integral. First flip the impulse response to form $h(-\tau)$. Next shift that flipped response by the fixed output time t to form $h(t-\tau)$. Then multiply it by $x(\tau)$. Finally, integrate the product over $\tau$.

The important point is that $h(t-\tau)$ is not drawn by moving $\tau$ itself. You choose one value of t, keep that value fixed, and view $h(t-\tau)$ as the flipped impulse response shifted along the $\tau$-axis.

This lesson uses the procedure to set up $y(t)$. Later work can focus on identifying overlap intervals and evaluating the integral, but the setup always follows the same order: flip, shift, multiply, integrate.

sections.section_title: Flipping the Impulse Response in $\tau$

image_slots.image_description: A two-panel worked-example graph on horizontal tau-axes. The top panel is labeled h(tau) and shows an asymmetric finite-duration signal with support from tau=1 to tau=3: height 1 on 1 <= tau < 2 and height 2 on 2 <= tau <= 3, zero elsewhere. Mark landmarks tau=1, tau=2, tau=3 and amplitudes 1 and 2. Draw a vertical dashed reflection axis at tau=0. The bottom panel is labeled h(-tau) and shows the reflected signal with support from tau=-3 to tau=-1: height 2 on -3 <= tau < -2 and height 1 on -2 <= tau <= -1, zero elsewhere. Mark landmarks tau=-3, tau=-2, tau=-1. Include small mapping labels 1 -> -1, 2 -> -2, and 3 -> -3. Do not include x(tau), h(t-tau), overlap shading, multiplication, or integration.

example_content.example_prompt: Given a plotted impulse response $h(\tau)$ with support from $\tau=1$ to $\tau=3$, sketch $h(-\tau)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the negative sign inside $h(-\tau)$. That negative sign reflects the graph horizontally across $\tau=0$. The time locations change sign, but the heights of the graph stay the same.
Start by marking the original support endpoints and any shape landmarks. In this example, $h(\tau)$ is nonzero from $\tau=1$ to $\tau=3$, with a visible landmark at $\tau=2$.
After the reflection, the support runs from $\tau=-3$ to $\tau=-1$. The part that was farther to the right moves farther to the left, and each amplitude is redrawn at its reflected $\tau$-location.
Label the reflected graph $h(-\tau)$. This is only the flip step of the convolution setup, so t has not been used yet and $h(t-\tau)$ has not been formed.

sections.section_title: Shifting the Flipped Impulse Response by Fixed $t$

image_slots.image_description: A two-panel worked-example graph on horizontal tau-axes. The top panel is labeled h(-tau) and shows the already-flipped impulse response with support from tau=-3 to tau=-1: height 2 on -3 <= tau < -2 and height 1 on -2 <= tau <= -1, zero elsewhere. Mark landmarks tau=-3, tau=-2, tau=-1 and amplitudes 2 and 1. Add a fixed label t=2 and a rightward shift arrow labeled shift right by 2. The bottom panel is labeled h(2-tau) and shows the same shape shifted right by 2, with support from tau=-1 to tau=1: height 2 on -1 <= tau < 0 and height 1 on 0 <= tau <= 1, zero elsewhere. Mark landmarks tau=-1, tau=0, tau=1. Include mapping labels -3 -> -1, -2 -> 0, and -1 -> 1. Do not include x(tau), overlap shading, multiplication, or integration.

example_content.example_prompt: Starting from a plotted $h(-\tau)$, sketch $h(2-\tau)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the fixed number in $h(2-\tau)$. Treat t as the fixed value 2, then move the already-flipped graph $h(-\tau)$ along the $\tau$-axis. Since $h(2-\tau)=h(-(\tau-2)$), the graph of $h(-\tau)$ shifts right by 2.
Start with the landmarks of the current $h(-\tau)$ graph. Here the support runs from $\tau=-3$ to $\tau=-1$, with a visible landmark at $\tau=-2$.
Shift every $\tau$-location in the flipped graph by 2 units to the right. The landmarks move as follows, and the amplitudes do not change.
So the shifted support is $\tau=-1$ to $\tau=1$, with the same shape and the same heights as the starting $h(-\tau)$ graph.
Label the result $h(2-\tau)$. This step only uses the fixed value $t=2$ to position the flipped response; $x(\tau)$, multiplication, and integration have not been introduced yet.

sections.section_title: Multiplying $x(\tau)$ by $h(t-\tau)$

image_slots.image_description: A three-panel worked-example graph on aligned horizontal tau-axes. The top panel is labeled x(tau) and shows a rectangular signal of height 2 on 0 <= tau <= 2, zero elsewhere. The middle panel is labeled h(2-tau) and shows the shifted response from the prior example: height 2 on -1 <= tau < 0, height 1 on 0 <= tau <= 1, zero elsewhere. Mark the overlap interval 0 <= tau <= 1 on the shared tau-axis. The bottom panel is labeled p(tau)=x(tau)h(2-tau) and shows the product signal: height 2 on 0 <= tau <= 1, zero elsewhere. Include a small annotation on the overlap reading 2 times 1 equals 2. Do not include an integral sign, area computation, y(t), or any candidate answer choices.

example_content.example_prompt: For plotted rectangular $x(\tau)$ and plotted $h(2-\tau)$ on the same $\tau$-axis, sketch $x(\tau)h(2-\tau)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both factors are now drawn on the same $\tau$-axis. To form $x(\tau)$$h(2-\tau)$, keep only $\tau$-values where both signals are nonzero, then multiply the two heights point by point.
From the plots, $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0 \le \tau \le 2$. The shifted response $h(2-\tau)$ is nonzero on $-1 \le \tau \le 1$.
So the product can only be nonzero on $0 \le \tau \le 1$. On that overlap, the plotted height of $x(\tau)$ is 2 and the plotted height of $h(2-\tau)$ is 1, so the product height is 2.
Outside the overlap, at least one factor is zero, so the product is zero. The product signal is therefore a rectangle of height 2 on $0 \le \tau \le 1$.
Label this product graph $x(\tau)$$h(2-\tau)$. This section forms the product only; the next step is where that product would be integrated over $\tau$.

sections.section_title: Integrating the Product Over $\tau$

image_slots.image_description: A single worked-example graph on a horizontal tau-axis showing the product signal p(tau)=x(tau)h(2-tau). The product is a rectangle of height 2 on 0 <= tau <= 1 and zero elsewhere. Shade the rectangle over 0 <= tau <= 1. Label the left endpoint tau=0, right endpoint tau=1, height 2, and width 1. Add an integral label int_{-infty}^{infty} p(tau) d tau and a small area annotation 2 times 1 equals 2. Do not show the original x(tau) or h(2-tau) plots, answer choices, or any full y(t) curve.

example_content.example_prompt: For the plotted product $p(\tau)=x(\tau)h(2-\tau)$, compute $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(\tau)\,d\tau$.

explanation_blocks.text: The product signal has already been formed. At this stage, t is fixed at 2, and the remaining job is to integrate the product over $\tau$. For a plotted product, that means finding the signed area under $p(\tau)$.
From the plot, $p(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $0 \le \tau \le 1$. On that interval, the product height is 2.
Because $p(\tau)$ is zero outside that interval, the integral over all $\tau$ reduces to the area of one rectangle.
So the product contributes 2 to the convolution output at this fixed value of t.

sections.section_title: Setting Up the Full Convolution Output

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=1$ for $0\le t\le 2$ and $0$ otherwise, and $h(t)=e^{-t}$ for $t\ge 0$ and $0$ otherwise, write the convolution setup for $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$ as an integral over $\tau$ without evaluating it.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the prompt asks for the convolution setup, not the evaluated output. Use the flip-shift-multiply-integrate form by rewriting the input as $x(\tau)$, rewriting the impulse-response factor as $h(t-\tau)$, multiplying those two factors, and integrating over $\tau$.
First rewrite the input using $\tau$ as the variable. The original formula for $x(t)$ becomes the same rectangular rule on the $\tau$-axis.

Next form the shifted flipped impulse-response factor by substituting t-$\tau$ into h. Since $h(u)=e$^{-u} for u greater than or equal to 0, the factor $h(t-\tau)$ equals $e^{-(t-\tau)}$ when t-$\tau$ is nonnegative, and equals 0 otherwise.
Now multiply the two $\tau$-dependent factors and place the product inside the convolution integral. Keep the limits from negative infinity to infinity because this is only the setup step.
This is the full convolution setup. It identifies $x(\tau)$, forms $h(t-\tau)$, multiplies the factors, and integrates over $\tau$, but it does not analyze overlap intervals or evaluate the integral.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret each convolution output value as the signed area of the product over the tau-interval where x(tau) overlaps the flipped-shifted impulse response h(t-tau).

sections.section_title: Introduction to Convolution as Overlap Area

image_slots.image_description: A clean instructional convolution-overlap diagram on a shared tau-axis. Show a simple positive rectangular x(tau) pulse and a simple positive rectangular flipped-shifted h(t0-tau) pulse for one fixed output time t=t0. Shade only the interval where the two rectangles overlap. Below them, show the product x(tau)h(t0-tau) as one positive rectangle over the same overlap interval. Label the shaded product area as y(t0). Include clear labels for tau, x(tau), h(t0-tau), x(tau)h(t0-tau), the overlap interval, and the area that becomes y(t0). Keep the signals simple and avoid moving-t case boundaries or a full convolution-output plot.

blocks.text: The convolution integral can be read as an area calculation when the output time is fixed. For one chosen value of t, $\tau$ is the variable that runs along the signal timeline.

At that fixed output time, the two factors $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ only contribute on $\tau$-values where both signals are nonzero. Outside their overlap, at least one factor is zero, so the product contributes no area.

On the overlap interval, multiply the two signal values point by point. This creates the product signal $x(\tau)$$h(t-\tau)$. The signed area under that product, measured along the $\tau$-axis, is the single output value for the chosen time.

If the product is above the axis, its area adds to $y(t)$. If the product is below the axis, its area subtracts from $y(t)$. If there is no overlap, the product is zero everywhere, so that output value is zero.
In this lesson, the main task is to read convolution output values from overlap area. The focus is the area of the product for one fixed output time, not the full piecewise convolution curve.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Product Area for a Fixed Output Time

image_slots.image_description: Two aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared tau-axis for fixed output time t=2. Top plot: x(tau)=1 on 0<=tau<=3 and 0 elsewhere. Middle plot: h(2-tau)=2 on 1<=tau<=4 and 0 elsewhere. Shade the overlap interval 1<=tau<=3 on both plots. Bottom product-area panel: show x(tau)h(2-tau)=2 on 1<=tau<=3 and 0 elsewhere as a rectangle of width 2 and height 2, shaded and labeled area = 4 = y(2). Include tau-axis labels and endpoints 0, 1, 3, and 4.

example_content.example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=2$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(2-\tau)=2$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Interpret $y(2)$ as an overlap area.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that $t$ is already fixed at 2. That means $h(2-\tau)$ is a fixed shifted response, and the only variable being scanned is $\tau$.
Read the two nonzero intervals from the graph. The input $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 3$, and the shifted response $h(2-\tau)$ is nonzero on $1\le \tau\le 4$.
The product can be nonzero only where both intervals are active. The common part is $1\le \tau\le 3$.
On that overlap, $x(\tau)=1$ and $h(2-\tau)=2$, so the product height is 2. The overlap width is $3-1=2$.
The output value $y(2)$ is the signed area under the product over the overlap interval. Here the product is positive, so the area is positive.
So for this fixed output time, the overlap area gives $y(2)=4$.

sections.section_title: Reading Positive Overlap Area from Two Positive Signals

image_slots.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared tau-axis for fixed output time t=3. Top plot: x(tau)=2 on 0<=tau<=4 and 0 elsewhere, entirely above the axis. Middle plot: h(3-tau)=1 on 1<=tau<=3 and 0 elsewhere, entirely above the axis. Shade the overlap interval 1<=tau<=3 on both plots. Bottom product-area panel: show x(tau)h(3-tau)=2 on 1<=tau<=3 and 0 elsewhere as a rectangle above the axis with width 2, height 2, and positive area label +4 = y(3). Include tau-axis labels and endpoints 0, 1, 3, and 4.

example_content.example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=3$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(3-\tau)=1$ on $1\le \tau\le 3$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the overlap area to find $y(3)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both plotted signals are above the axis wherever they overlap. When both signal values are positive, their product is positive, so the overlap area adds to the convolution output.
Read the overlap interval from the two supports. The signal $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 4$, and $h(3-\tau)$ is nonzero on $1\le \tau\le 3$. Their common interval is $1\le \tau\le 3$.
On this overlap, the heights are $x(\tau)=2$ and $h(3-\tau)=1$. Multiplying two positive heights gives a positive product height.
The product rectangle has width $3-1=2$ and height 2. Because the rectangle is above the axis, its signed area is positive.
So the positive overlap area contributes $+4$, and the convolution output at this fixed time is $y(3)=4$.

sections.section_title: Accounting for Signed Area When the Product Is Negative

image_slots.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared tau-axis for fixed output time t=1. Top plot: x(tau)=2 on 0<=tau<=3 and 0 elsewhere, entirely above the axis. Middle plot: h(1-tau)=-1 on 1<=tau<=4 and 0 elsewhere, entirely below the axis on its support. Shade the overlap interval 1<=tau<=3 on both plots. Bottom product-area panel: show x(tau)h(1-tau)=-2 on 1<=tau<=3 and 0 elsewhere as a rectangle below the axis with width 2, height -2, and signed area label -4 = y(1). Include tau-axis labels and endpoints 0, 1, 3, and 4.

example_content.example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=1$, a graph shows $x(\tau)=2$ on $0\le \tau\le 3$ and $h(1-\tau)=-1$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$, with both signals zero elsewhere. Use the signed overlap area to find $y(1)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the two overlapping signal values have opposite signs. The overlap area is still found the same way as before, but the product lies below the axis, so its signed area is negative.
Read the two nonzero intervals from the graph. The input $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on $0\le \tau\le 3$, and the shifted response $h(1-\tau)$ is nonzero on $1\le \tau\le 4$.
On the overlap, $x(\tau)=2$ is positive and $h(1-\tau)=-1$ is negative. The sign of the area comes from the sign of their product.
The product rectangle has width $3-1=2$ and height $-2$. Since the product is below the axis, the signed area is negative.
So the signed overlap area contributes $-4$, and the convolution output at this fixed time is $y(1)=-4$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Output Values from Different Amounts of Overlap

image_slots.image_description: Two side-by-side fixed-output-time panels on shared tau-axes. In both panels, show the same x(tau)=1 on 1<=tau<=4 and 0 elsewhere. Left panel labeled t=1: show h(1-tau)=2 on -1<=tau<=2 and 0 elsewhere, shade overlap 1<=tau<=2, and show a product-area rectangle x(tau)h(1-tau)=2 on 1<=tau<=2 with area 2 labeled y(1)=2. Right panel labeled t=3: show h(3-tau)=2 on 1<=tau<=4 and 0 elsewhere, shade overlap 1<=tau<=4, and show a product-area rectangle x(tau)h(3-tau)=2 on 1<=tau<=4 with area 6 labeled y(3)=6. Use matching positive colors for product regions above the axis and include a comparison label y(3)>y(1).

example_content.example_prompt: Two panels show the same input $x(\tau)=1$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$ with $h(1-\tau)=2$ on $-1\le \tau\le 2$ in the first panel and $h(3-\tau)=2$ on $1\le \tau\le 4$ in the second panel, with all signals zero elsewhere. Compare $y(1)$ and $y(3)$ by comparing the two overlap areas.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that each panel represents a different fixed output time. Use the same signed-area rule in each panel, then compare the resulting product areas.
For the first panel, the fixed output time is $t=1$. The input is active on $1\le \tau\le 4$, while $h(1-\tau)$ is active on $-1\le \tau\le 2$, so the overlap is $1\le \tau\le 2$.
On that overlap, the product height is $1\cdot 2=2$. The overlap width is $2-1=1$, so the signed product area is positive and equals 2.
For the second panel, the fixed output time is $t=3$. The same input is active on $1\le \tau\le 4$, and $h(3-\tau)$ is also active on $1\le \tau\le 4$, so the overlap is wider.
The product height is still $1\cdot 2=2$, but the overlap width is $4-1=3$. That gives a larger positive product area.
Both product areas are positive, so the larger area gives the larger output value. Therefore, $y(3)>y(1)$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Zero Output from No Overlap Area

image_slots.image_description: Aligned rectangular signal plots on a shared tau-axis for fixed output time t=5. Top plot: x(tau) is supported on 0<=tau<=2 and zero elsewhere. Middle plot: h(5-tau) is supported on 3<=tau<=4 and zero elsewhere. Leave a visible gap between tau=2 and tau=3 and label it no overlap. Do not shade any common interval. Bottom product-area panel: show x(tau)h(5-tau)=0 for all tau, with no product rectangle and a label area = 0 = y(5). Include tau-axis labels and endpoints 0, 2, 3, and 4.

example_content.example_prompt: At fixed output time $t=5$, a graph shows $x(\tau)$ supported on $0\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(5-\tau)$ supported on $3\le \tau\le 4$. Use overlap area to determine $y(5)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the two nonzero support intervals are separated. The output does not come from the area of either individual signal; it comes from the signed area of the product where both signals are nonzero at the same $\tau$-values.
Read the two supports from the graph. The input $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $0\le \tau\le 2$, and the shifted response $h(5-\tau)$ is nonzero only on $3\le \tau\le 4$.

explanation_blocks.latex: x(\tau)\ne 0\text{ only on }0\le \tau\le 2,\qquad h(5-\tau)\ne 0\text{ only on }3\le \tau\le 4

explanation_blocks.text: These intervals do not overlap. There is a gap between the end of the support of $x(\tau)$ and the start of the support of $h(5-\tau)$.
Since there is no $\tau$-value where both factors are nonzero, their product is zero for every value of $\tau$.
The signed area under a product that is zero everywhere is zero. Therefore the convolution output at this fixed time is $y(5)=0$.
